newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO prepares for more talks with Russia.
newsitem.headline: NATO prepares for more talks with Russia.

text.p: With the pace of diplomacy quickening, NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana prepared on Saturday for a second round of talks with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov on a new NATO-Russia relationship.
The talks on a new charter or treaty to gain Moscow's backing for the alliance's plans to expand into former communist central and eastern Europe will take place in Brussels on Sunday.
NATO, with Moscow's backing, has imposed a total news blackout on the meeting which authoritative sources say will take place over dinner at Solana's Brussels residence.
The meeting, a follow-up to one last month, follows a week of intensive diplomacy which saw the U.S. Secretary of State, and the Italian and German foreign ministers in Moscow.
On the surface, there has been no progress towards removing Moscow's determined opposition to enlargement -- an issue which unites Russia's entire political class.

But behind Moscow's strident public rhetoric, alliance diplomats say there has been an acceptance they cannot stop some form of limited enlargement and are about to enter into a real dialogue on an overall NATO-Russia deal.
NATO intends to invite new members into the alliance that won the Cold War at a summit in Madrid in July. At the same summit, they would like to endorse the new NATO-Russia charter.
But the Western allies have made clear enlargement -- led by Poland, Hungary, and the Czech Republic -- will take place whatever happens.
"Not to enlarge is the do-nothing, achieve-nothing option. It is the option the alliance long ago rejected," Solana told a conference on European security in Brussels on Friday.

After weeks of concessions by the allies, Solana -- who has been mandated to negotiate the deal -- is expected to move onto the offensive and push Primakov to detail what Russia can bring to any new relationship.

"When are they going to ratify START 2 (a key arms control deal), what can they bring to an 'open skies' deal, reciprocal consultation and military liaison? He will push them on these, it is not one-way any more," said one senior diplomat.
Alliance sources say Solana is also likely to tell Primakov NATO has no objections to an earlier special NATO-Russia summit to formalise the agreement if that is more to Moscow's liking.

President Boris Yeltsin inisted in a 15-minute telephone conversation earlier this week with German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel that any treaty or charter should be enshrined in a legally-binding document.

Solana is expected to try and move the debate more on to the content rather than the form of any charter, arguing the document can be flexible and commit states politically without having to go before every country's parliament.
"The Helsinki Final Document was not legally binding, but no-one questioned its validity," said another senior diplomatic source.
Some NATO states, however, are prepared to take legal advice over whether there is some options between a "treaty and a purely political document".

Washington's new Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said talks this week in Rome, Paris, Bonn, Brussels, London and Moscow had brought no breakthrough, but said importaqnt progress had been made towards overcoming Russia's hostility.
Primakov repeated Moscow's opposition but said he wanted to "minimise complications" if NATO's plan went ahead.
